newsitem.title: USA: EPA defends long deadlines for new clean air rules.
newsitem.headline: EPA defends long deadlines for new clean air rules.

text.p: A senior U.S. environmental official on Thursday defended the government's drawn-out schedule for cities and counties to meet strict new smog and soot standards, saying the lag would give businesses time to plan to meet the new targets.

The Environmental Protection Agency last week issued a tough new limit on smog-forming ozone to go into effect in 2004 and a brand new standard for fine particles, or soot, to go into effect in 2005, both of which would not be enforced until several years later.

Opponents of the rules, worried about the potentially high costs of new pollution controls, criticised the agency for setting standards that would not be enforced for many years while at the same time claiming they were urgently needed to save lives.

In response, EPA Assistant Administrator Mary Nichols said the standards had to be set so businesses could start planning how to clean up their operations. "Without a goal, people don't know where they're trying to head," she said.
"Having the standard out there, as we have done, gives them that target," she told the Senate clean air subcommittee.

Inhofe and other Republicans accused the administration of lying to counties, farmers and small businesses in reassuring them that utilities and big industrial plants would shoulder most of the costs of cleaning the air.
"How can you say this is not going to affect small businesses if their electric rates are going to go up between eight and 11 percent?" said panel chairman Inhofe.
Sen. Tim Hutchinson, Republican of Arkansas, said if power plants had to spend more to curb their emissions, they would simply pass the costs on to ratepayers.

But Nichols said ratepayers would not necessarily see higher rates, because the new pollution curbs would come into effect at the same time as the power industry was being deregulated, which would bring rates down.
"As competition becomes more prevalent (in the power industry) there's a great opportunity to both reduce the costs of electricity and reduce pollution," she said.
